title: How to research a company with AI
description: Research one company across current public and authorized sources, then turn the strongest findings into a concise, source-linked brief.
introduction: Ask most AI tools about a company and the answer comes back in the same shape every time: what it does, roughly how big it is, when it raised money, a few recent headlines. That is reasonable background, and it is almost never the thing you needed. If you are deciding whether to build on someone's API, the question that matters is how often it breaks and how they behave when it does—which no company profile contains.

Strawberry can research a company the way you would with an afternoon to spend on it: reading the documentation, working through sites and tools you already have access to, opening sources you might not have thought to check, and comparing all of it against files or data you provide. What comes back is an answer to the question you actually asked, with the sources sitting next to the claims.

sections.title: Start with the question, not the company

blocks.text: The same company supports very different investigations. Sizing up a potential vendor means looking hard at reliability, support, pricing history, and who else already depends on them. Understanding a competitor who has just entered your market is closer to product detail, hiring, and where their attention is going. Reading up on a company before a first conversation may need nothing more than a current, accurate picture of what they actually sell.

So it helps to say what you are deciding and how much the answer is worth. A bounded question should come back quickly with something useful. A consequential one deserves a second pass into the places where the evidence is still thin.
Ask your Strawberry companion to research the company around that question, and it will work through the sources with you rather than handing back a profile.

items.context: Research this company around the question or decision I need help with.

blocks.text: A company's marketing pages tell you what it wants understood, which is rarely the thing you came to find out. The more useful material usually sits further in—a changelog that shows how fast the product really moves, documentation that reveals what the integration will actually require, a status history, a pricing page read against the version archived last year, a support forum where the same complaint keeps reappearing.

Most of that is reachable but tedious. Some of it sits behind a login you already have: an analyst database your team subscribes to, a procurement portal, a shared drive holding last year's evaluation. Strawberry can work through both—following a promising link several levels down, searching inside a site rather than around it, and using the sources you are authorized to use—then bring what it finds together with the public web. You don't have to work out in advance which sources will matter and paste them in.

sections.title: Keep the gaps and contradictions visible

blocks.text: A brief earns its length by being clear about what it knows. It should be obvious which claims are the company's own, which are corroborated somewhere independent, which are inference, and where the evidence simply isn't there yet.

items: The clearest answer to the question you started with.
The company context needed to understand that answer.
Source links and dates beside the findings that matter.
Contradictions, gaps, and useful questions to investigate next.

blocks.text: Contradictions are worth more than they first appear. When a company's job postings and its published roadmap disagree about where the product is going, that gap is often the most useful line in the brief—and it only shows up if the two sources are read against each other rather than summarized separately.

sections.title: Know when it's really a sales or investment question

blocks.text: A general brief stops at a clear, source-linked view of the company. Some decisions carry their own discipline behind them—running a deal, testing a fund's thesis—and those are better served by the workflow built for them than by one brief stretched to cover everything.

items.title: For a sales account
items.text: Combine what you found with the relationship, stakeholders, and most useful sales next step.

skill.context: Research this company as an account and relationship for the sales decision ahead.

items.title: For an investment screen
items.text: Assess the preliminary thesis fit, tensions, risks, and questions worth resolving next.

skill.context: Research this company as an investment opportunity and show what deserves deeper attention.

sections.title: Finish the research before you design the deck

blocks.text: Research and design are separate jobs. When they run together the research tends to lose, because slides that look finished are easy to mistake for questions that are settled. Once the company view is accepted, Strawberry can build the presentation from it without reopening the investigation.

items.context: Turn this accepted company brief into a polished, source-grounded presentation.

blocks.text: If your team researches companies the same way repeatedly, the accepted sources, questions, depth, and brief format can be saved as a shared skill. A recurring update can become a Routine once the sources, the changes worth tracking, the cadence, and the review point are clear.
